summary: Defines managed objects for devices that implement FDDI, a fiber-optic ring network, based on the ANSI FDDI Station Management specification, so they can be monitored with SNMP. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1512 defines the management objects for FDDI, the fibre-optic token ring network. It is mostly a translation: the American National Standards Institute had already worked out what information an FDDI machine should report about its ring, its MAC layer, its paths and its ports, and this memo rewrites those definitions in the format SNMP uses, without changing what they mean.

subtitle: Managed objects for FDDI fibre rings, recast from the ANSI station management standard.

tldr.problem: The ANSI committee had already defined how a fibre ring's station management, MAC, path and port layers should be described. Those definitions were not in the form SNMP could use, so there was no standard way to manage an FDDI machine over the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo takes the ANSI FDDI SMT 7.3 objects and recasts them in the Internet's SMI, keeping the meanings unchanged and changing only the syntax: booleans become enumerated integers and bit strings become octet strings. The result is a MIB module with five groups, holding the station's own configuration, the MAC, an optional set of extra MAC counters, and the paths and ports of the ring.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1512 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It updates RFC 1285, and says plainly that no assumptions should be made about compatibility with it, because the objects sit on a different branch of the MIB tree.

sections.title: The Framework and the Object Definitions
sections.content:
The Internet-standard Network Management Framework has three components: STD 16, RFC 1155, which defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management, with STD 16, RFC 1212 defining a more concise description mechanism wholly consistent with the SMI; STD 17, RFC 1213, which defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols; and STD 15, RFC 1157, which defines SNMP, the protocol used for network access to managed objects. The framework permits new objects to be defined for the purpose of experimentation and evaluation.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. Objects in the MIB are defined using the subset of Abstract Syntax Notation One defined in the SMI. Each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name, and the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object. For human convenience a textual string, termed the descriptor, is often used to refer to the object type. The object types in this MIB module are defined using the conventions of the SMI, as amended by the extensions specified in the extended OBJECT-TYPE macro.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP management works by naming each piece of information a device can report with a number called an object identifier, and by grouping related names into tables. This memo adds one more table group for FDDI equipment to the set already defined for the Internet protocols.

sections.title: Overview and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The memo defines the managed objects for FDDI devices accessible via SNMP, applying at present to interfaces whose ifType value in the Internet-standard MIB is fddi, which has the value 15. For these interfaces the ifSpecific variable in MIB-II has the object identifier value fddimib, which is fddi 73.

The definitions draw heavily on related work in the ANSI X3T9.5 committee and the SMT subcommittee of that committee. In fact, the definitions of the managed objects in the memo are, to the maximum extent possible, identical to those identified by the ANSI committee. The semantics of each managed object should be the same, with syntactic changes made as necessary to recast the objects in terms of the Internet-standard SMI and MIB so as to be compatible with SNMP. Examples of these syntactic changes include remapping booleans to enumerated integers and remapping bit strings to octet strings. The naming of the objects was also changed to achieve compatibility. These minimal syntactic changes with no semantic changes should allow implementations of SNMP manageable FDDI systems to share instrumentation with other network management schemes and thereby minimise implementation cost, and the translation of information conveyed by managed objects from one network management scheme to another is eased by the shared definitions.

Only the essential variables, as indicated by their mandatory status in the ANSI specification, were retained, because the importance of variables with an optional status in the ANSI specification was perceived to be less widely accepted.

Several new datatypes are introduced as textual conventions, which enhance the readability of the document and ease comparisons with the ANSI counterpart. Their introduction has no effect on either the syntax or the semantics of any managed object: objects defined in terms of one of them are always encoded by the rules that define the primitive type, so no changes to the SMI or SNMP are needed.

The conventions are FddiTimeNano, an integer from 0 to 2147483647 specifying 1 nanosecond units, with the note that the encoding is normal integer representation and not two's complement, so converting an ANSI variable requires two operations: converting from two's complement to normal integer representation, and multiplying by 80 to convert from 80 nanosecond units to 1 nanosecond units; FddiTimeMilli, an integer from 0 to 2147483647 giving time in 1 millisecond units; FddiResourceId, an integer from 0 to 65535 used to refer to an instance of a MAC, PORT or PATH resource identifier, where indexing begins at 1 and zero indicates the absence of a resource; FddiSMTStationIdType, an octet string of 8 octets representing the unique identifier of the FDDI station, in which the low order 6 octets come from a unique IEEE assigned address and the first two octets are implementor-defined; and FddiMACLongAddressType, an octet string of 6 octets holding a long MAC address in the IEEE canonical notation for 48 bit addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects themselves come from the ANSI standard, so an FDDI device already knows what to report. What the memo changes is the encoding, so that SNMP can carry it: a yes or no becomes a numbered value, and a field of bits becomes a string of bytes. The times are also converted, from the 80 nanosecond units FDDI uses to ordinary nanoseconds or milliseconds, so that a manager reads plain numbers.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1285
sections.content: The changes from RFC 1285 to this memo, based on the changes from ANSI SMT 6.2 to SMT 7.3, were so numerous that the objects in this MIB module are located on a different branch of the MIB tree. No assumptions should be made about compatibility with RFC 1285.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version of this MIB was based on an older version of the ANSI standard, and so many objects changed that the memo had to move the whole set to a new place in the tree of names. A manager written against the old version will not find the objects where it expects.

sections.title: The Five Groups of Objects
sections.content:
The module is named FDDI-SMT73-MIB and holds five groups. The first four are named by their object identifiers: fddimibSMT, fddimibMAC, fddimibMACCounters, fddimibPATH and fddimibPORT, under the fddimib identifier which is fddi 73.

The SMT group holds information common to a station management entity, the part of FDDI that decides how the ring is used. Its implementation is mandatory for all systems which implement manageable FDDI subsystems. A table of SMT entries is indexed by an SMT index, and the number of entries must not exceed the value of fddimibSMTNumber, which counts the number of SMT implementations on the entity regardless of their current state and must stay the same across a re-initialisation. An SMT entry carries the station identifier, the operation, high and low version identifiers, user data, the MIB version identifier, the number of MACs, non-master connections and master connections, the number of available paths, the configuration capabilities, the configuration policy, the connection policy, the notification setting, the statistics reporting policy, the maximum trace expiration time, whether a bypass is present, and the ECM and CF states.

The MAC group holds information about the medium access control layer, and its implementation is likewise mandatory for all systems which implement manageable FDDI subsystems. A table of MAC entries is indexed by the SMT index and the MAC index, and the number of entries must not exceed the value of fddimibMACNumber, which counts the total number of MAC implementations across all SMTs on the entity.

The Enhanced MAC Counters group is optional, but systems claiming support must implement all the variables in it. It holds a table of MAC counters entries indexed by the SMT index and the MAC index, with the number of entries not exceeding the MAC number.

The PATH group is mandatory for all systems which implement manageable FDDI subsystems. It describes the paths, the logical connections between stations around the ring, with a table of path entries and a count of the total number of paths possible across all SMTs.

The PORT group is also mandatory for all systems which implement manageable FDDI subsystems. It describes the ports, the physical attachments to the ring, with a table of port entries and a count of the total number of port implementations across all SMTs.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects fall into five groups. SMT covers the station's own configuration, such as how many connections it makes and what policy it follows. MAC covers the medium access control layer. PATH covers the logical connections around the ring, and PORT covers the physical attachments to it. Four of the five groups are mandatory for any FDDI device that is manageable at all; the extra MAC counters are optional, and a device that claims them must provide all of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo has a Security Considerations section, and its entire content is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

Nothing in the document describes authentication, access control or confidentiality for the management information it defines. The objects are counters, identifiers, states and policies, and the memo says nothing about who may read them or change them.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed, so nothing in it should be read as a claim that the management information is protected.
